results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec
All 58 aligned units' outline summaries match their spec paragraphs' controlling ideas in spec order; the five callouts carry the roadmap and thesis as the spec's introduction places them.

results.draft_locus: Introduction ¶1
results.quote: Part IV argues that most discovery queries are filters in disguise, and that the platform should compile a buyer's words, places and saved searches into its own structure; this chapter does that for place.
results.finding: The outliner needed two phrases. Besides p01's idea (place is the first filter, so the map needs its own ranking and evaluation, stated twice: at the opening and again after the place-first argument), the paragraph ends with a separate Part IV framing claim that p01 does not hold.

Worked Example: The Lyon Apartment on the Map ¶3 was marked two ideas (value of one compiler, value of entity resolution), but p46 declares both as one analysis, 'what the example shows', and the paragraph opens by announcing exactly that; it reads as one idea with two coordinated parts.
Every unit ties to one of S1-S6 or to the introduction/conclusion functions declared in the spec; no orphan paragraph.

results.draft_locus: Commute Search: Isochrones and Travel Times ¶8
results.quote: that is 270 requests per second, each needing an isochrone and a travel-time matrix for its pins
results.finding: The arithmetic is correct (10% of 2,700 = 270; 30% misses of 270 = 81, about 80; 270 x 50 x 1-2 = 13,500-27,000), but the assumption behind it is not explained and contradicts the chapter: the commute table and p32 say an isochrone is computed once per search, while here every commute-session map request needs one. The spec's reasoning ('a new isochrone per parameter change and a matrix per page') is not stated, so a reader cannot see why 80 isochrones/s is the right load. The next sentence ('If each matrix times 50 pins (the largest list page)') does not parse and mixes map pins with a list page.

Other evidence items are followed or framed by a sentence saying what they show: the five-ways table (traps 'inside the table'), the list/map table ('Two consequences follow'), the commute-patterns table (next paragraph says why both are needed), the verticals table ('As the table below shows'), Figures 1-5, the Airbnb, Rightmove and TravelTime quotations, and the polygon figures (146->31 vertices, 1.8 s->240 ms, checked).

results.draft_locus: Introduction ¶1
results.quote: [[recommendations]] showed that a surface buyers browse without typing a query still needs its own ranking and evaluation; the map is another such surface.
results.finding: The similarity with recommendations is expressed, but the spec says the claim for the map is stated after the place-first argument; the draft states it at the start and again after the argument ('So the map, like the recommendation surfaces, needs its own ranking and evaluation'), so the opening sentence asserts before it argues.

results.draft_locus: Five Ways to Say "Here" ¶1
results.quote: Buyers express place in five ways.
results.finding: Declared: sequence, carrying over Ingrid's first question (which query shapes the map needs). The section opens with a bare statement; nothing ties the five expressions to the first question, so the reader is not told this section begins the answer.

results.draft_locus: Architecture: A Geo Query Compiler in Front of the Engine ¶1
results.quote: The design I recommend puts a geo query compiler between the map clients and the engine, and gives each remaining map concern its own component with a narrow interface.
results.finding: Declared: problem_solution, carrying over the map as a separate product with many small queries. The opening does not pick up the previous section's conclusion (a search client in its own right with its own query mix), so the compiler is not presented as the answer to that problem.

results.draft_locus: Performance and Caching at the Peak ¶1
results.quote: Map traffic peaks with all search traffic.
results.finding: Declared: sequence, carrying over the compiler's inputs and the data around them and introducing the load all of it must carry at the peak. The opening follows the fair-housing rule with no link back to the compiler, polygons, clusters, commute and neighborhood layers it now has to size.

All other declared transitions (intro p02-p04, scene p06-p09, p11-p13, map-product and p15-p16, p18-p21, polygons and p28-p30, clustering and p23-p26, commute and p32-p47, neighborhood and p39, p41-p43, worked example and p45-p46, trade-offs, verticals, failure modes, CA view, questions, conclusion) express the declared relationship at the boundary; the hand-off links saved-searches-and-alerts.

results.draft_locus: Introduction ¶1
results.quote: So the map, like the recommendation surfaces, needs its own ranking and evaluation
results.finding: Both readers met the map-needs-its-own-ranking claim twice in one paragraph, before the reason and after it, and had to re-read to see the middle is the reason.

results.draft_locus: Introduction ¶1
results.quote: Part IV argues that most discovery queries are filters in disguise
results.finding: Both readers could not tell whether Part IV is this chapter's part; the sentence is tacked onto a paragraph about ranking.

results.draft_locus: The Map Is a Different Product ¶1
results.quote: The five expressions meet buyers on the map.
results.finding: Reader A found the bridge weak and the section an interruption between the primitives and the compiler; reader B judged the position defensible but placed between Five Ways and the compiler, and both proposed moving it before Five Ways. The spec's order has a stated reason (vocabulary first, then the case for a separate architecture); the prose does not make it visible: the bridge names the five expressions but the section never uses them, and the next section does not pick up the map-as-product conclusion.
results.corroborated_by: Flow reader B, section 2 (The Map Is a Different Product) and reordering suggestion 1

Terms on does_not_know are introduced before or at first use (bounding box, map tile, isochrone, place ID, public point, geo_point/geo_shape, geotile_grid, geohex_grid, Douglas-Peucker, Valhalla, GTFS, NDCG). results.draft_locus: Commute Search: Isochrones and Travel Times ¶4
results.quote: Per request, per element of a matrix, or a fixed license.
results.finding: 'Travel-time matrix' (on does_not_know) is used in the prose without a definition (origins x destinations, priced per element); the commute table may define it but was not visible to the judge, so 'never given' cannot be confirmed. Neither flow reader reported the term itself as unexplained.
The introduction opens with a direct, disputable statement about place-first discovery and a scoped case; none of the weak patterns.
The conclusion answers the three questions with a synthesis and hands off; no 'in conclusion', no new subtopic, no grab bag.

States what no single section does (one component fixes polygons, privacy, duplicates and routing cost at once) and why it matters (Hearthly moves onto the shared platform without The Forced Fit; new place interfaces need no client rebuild).

Returns to Ingrid's three questions, the 1.8-second polygons and Agence Rhône Habitat's stacked pins; routing is answered as 'bought on a forecast of peak volumes', though the per-request quote is not named explicitly.

The cold reader predicted all sections in the roadmap's order and the evidence (Airbnb, Zillow, Rightmove, engine and routing docs, fictional Veldmark) and tone; it could not say what the three questions are or what neighborhood data covers, which the roadmap promises but need not give.

The reader built the compiler (place-ID filters, tile snapping, repair/simplify under a 64-vertex cap), pins from the public point counted per canonical property (one pin, three offers), cached isochrones keyed by a snapped origin plus matrices for pins on screen, and the routing choice from a peak-volume forecast against pricing and license. Matches expected; owner 'search platform' is implied by 'server-side' and not stated in the summary.

The reader named the cluster-of-one leak via centroids, heatmaps and vector-tile hits, the rule that every returned geometry comes from a deterministic public point, an API that cannot read the exact point, minimum counts per cell and a DPO-signed platform invariant. Matches expected.

The reader explained geography-led attention and pin selection, Airbnb's 2024 paper and 2025 review (80%, map-specific NDCG), the stated inference for portals, and contacts and saves per map session and time to shortlist. Matches expected; minor note that failure mode 9 says Airbnb's work 'shows' list metrics mislead without the inference caveat.
